title: Bright one, give us bright wealth

words.meaning: rich in men, with many sons

sandhi.rule: saḥ loses its visarga before a consonant

samasa.meaning: with many heroes, rich in sons

morphology.note: Vedic dative/locative of the first person plural, ‘to us’.
causative participle of √cit, ‘making itself perceived’: the wealth is conspicuous.

translation.literal: You, O bright one, bright, conspicuous [wealth] for us, O you of bright dominion, most bright, giving vigour, gleaming wealth, rich in men, great, O shining one, with shining [hymns], to the one who praises, bestow.
translation.readable: Bright god, bright in your rule, bring us wealth that shines and is seen, the brightest, full of strength; gleaming wealth, rich in sons and great — O shining one, give it to the one who praises you with shining hymns.

meaning: A prayer for wealth, built on one sound: citra, ‘bright’, comes five times and candra, ‘shining’, three, all around one request — give the singer bright, great wealth. It is a Ṛgveda verse (6.6.7), from a hymn whose first verse praises the ‘son of strength’, the purifying fire. In the Navagraha sūktam it is the third mantra for Ketu, before the salutation; the witness marks it as a ṛk and names the graha’s adhidevatā and pratyadhidevatā together.
in_the_rite: Step 9 (Ketu), third mantra. The use of a Vedic verse for a graha belongs to the later gṛhya tradition. The witness marks this verse (ऋक्), and it is not in the Taittirīya texts the edition draws on; its text is the Ṛgveda’s (GRETIL, without svara), and no commentary on it is in the edition’s sources.

notes.label: linguistic
notes.text: A triṣṭubh. The play on citra and candra runs through both lines.

notes.label: historical
notes.text: The witness S marks the verse as a ṛk; the base text here is GRETIL’s Ṛgveda (Aufrecht 1877), which carries no svara.
